main_concern: The amendment creates a contract-layer commitment to "complete revival" within the same framework (terminal-goals.json, contract lifecycle) that already gamed the terminal-complete declaration. The definition of "complete" remains document-based rather than machine-checkable. Without an executable definition of completeness (e.g., a role checklist with coverage tests that FAIL against the current kernel), the same premature-completion pattern can repeat: the amendment becomes another convincing document rather than a trigger for working code. The constraint "the fix must include runtime checks" is itself stated in a document — it has no enforcement mechanism.
minimum_fix: Before accepting the amendment or proceeding to implementation, require three concrete, non-document artifacts: (1) A machine-enumerable checklist of all old RedCap design elements to be restored (roles, workflows, orchestration hooks) — in code, not markdown. (2) At least one end-to-end role workflow test that runs against the current fsm.py kernel and demonstrably FAILS, proving the gap between "kernel complete" and "workflow complete." (3) A machine-checkable definition of "complete" — e.g., an enum or registry of required roles with a static coverage check that gates any future terminal-goal declaration. Until these exist, the amendment is itself a paperwork artifact.
missing_evidence: The concrete list of old RedCap design ideas to be restored — only 'Loom role orchestration' is named; the full scope of deferred designs is unknown

Whether current fsm.py architecture can support a full role-orchestration workflow machine or requires a fundamental rewrite (the constraint forbids bulk-reading the old repo, so revival may depend on incomplete memory)
At least one executable end-to-end test demonstrating the delta between current kernel capability and the claimed 'complete workflow machine' target
reality_delta: The documented reality (terminal-goals.json, recent commits claiming "completion" and "验收") says RedCap is terminal-complete. The user's intended reality says it is a minimum kernel missing entire design dimensions (Loom orchestration, role workflows). These two realities diverge. The amendment correctly identifies this divergence but does not yet contain the machinery to prevent it from recurring — the same gap between document-claims and code-reality persists. Notably, constraint #3 forbids "keeping claiming terminal completion while role workflow and complete design revival remain incomplete" — but this constraint is self-referential: it is a document prohibiting documents, with no executable enforcement.
top_risks: Amendment lifecycle degenerates into infinite paperwork: The RedCap framework (prism-request → prism-review → amendment → implementation → verification → prism-request) generates a document at each node. If the amendment produces concerns that feed into amendment revisions (rather than code), the loop continues without executable output.

Undefined completion target enables re-gaming: Without a machine-checkable spec for 'complete workflow machine,' any future implementation can be declared complete by redefining the target downward, exactly as happened with the minimum kernel. The same terminal-goals.json system that already failed will be asked to judge its own correction.

Constraint #4 ('Do not bulk-read the old RedCap repository') may make genuine revival impossible: If the old Loom/Layer B designs exist only in the old repo's code, and that code cannot be read, then the revival is limited to what the developer remembers — which is exactly how the minimum kernel posture developed in the first place.
